abstract: Communication between stem cells and their specialized niche microenvironments is vital for organism development and tissue homeostasis. However, mechanisms that limit intracellular signaling within a given niche and thus maintain stem cell fate are not fully understood. The Hippo and Ecdysone nuclear receptor (EcR) pathways are well conserved and individually required in niche cells for the establishment and maintenance of stem cell pools in Drosophila. These pathways are linked in the nucleus via a physical interaction between their respective transcriptional coactivators Yorkie (Yki) and Taiman (Tai). Within the female Drosophila germline niche, Yki and Tai each regulate behavior of stem cells and their progeny. It is not known whether these roles are mechanistically distinct or are a product of a physical interaction between Yki and Tai that enables a common niche-support role. Here we utilize a CRISPR mutant fly line containing a form of Tai unable to bind Yki (taiPPxA) to examine requirements for the Yki:Tai interaction in vivo. We find that the Yki:Tai interaction controls the GSC niche mainly through a role in escort cells (ECs), a key somatic cell-type that ensheathes the niche and regulates intercellular signaling. taiPPxA reduces EC cytoplasmic processes and allows the Dpp ligand to spread beyond its normally restricted range within the GSC niche, which elevates Dpp signaling and blocks differentiation of GSC progeny. In sum, these findings suggest that a Yki:Tai interaction facilitates crosstalk between the Hippo and EcR pathways within ECs and thus plays a critical role in maintaining intercellular signals that allow somatic cells to shape the niche microenvironment.
